findings.title: Device limit is bypassed after the first rejection because the local cache is populated before the store write
findings.body: `tagDeviceUI` writes the device key into `a.localCache` (`a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{})`) *before* calling `a.anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice`. When the device limit is reached, `CreateOrUpdateDevice` returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached` and `Anonymous.Authenticate` denies the request — but the key is already cached. Every subsequent request from the same device ID hits the `if _, ok := a.localCache.Get(key); ok { return nil }` early-return for the next 29 minutes, so `TagDevice` returns nil and the anonymous user is authenticated normally. The configured limit therefore only blocks a device's very first request and is effectively unenforced afterwards. The cache entry should only be set after a successful store write (and removed/not set on error).

findings.title: Check-then-insert race allows the device limit to be exceeded
findings.body: `CreateOrUpdateDevice` reads the current device count with `CountDevices` and then, if `count < s.deviceLimit`, performs an unconditional upsert. Multiple concurrent requests (and multiple Grafana instances sharing the database) can all observe `count == limit-1` and all insert, so the number of distinct anonymous devices can exceed `AnonymousDeviceLimit`. If the limit is meant to be a hard cap, the count and insert need to be in a single transaction/statement (e.g. an `INSERT ... SELECT ... WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) ...) < limit`) or the overshoot needs to be acknowledged as acceptable.

findings.title: rowsAffected == 0 is reported as ErrDeviceLimitReached, conflating distinct conditions
findings.body: `updateDevice` returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached` whenever the UPDATE affects zero rows. Zero rows also occurs when the row exists but its `updated_at` falls outside the `[now-30d, now+1m]` window, and on MySQL an UPDATE that writes values identical to the stored ones reports 0 affected rows (the driver does not enable CLIENT_FOUND_ROWS), which can happen when `updated_at` is truncated to second precision and the same device is written twice within the same second. In those cases an already-known device is incorrectly refused authentication with a "device limit reached" error. The limit-reached condition should be distinguished from "row not updated" (e.g. check existence explicitly or treat 0 rows for a pre-existing device as success).

findings.title: New auth.anonymous.device_limit key missing from conf/defaults.ini, breaking env-var override and documentation
findings.body: `cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit = anonSection.Key("device_limit").MustInt64(0)` adds a new configuration key, but `conf/defaults.ini` (and `conf/sample.ini`) are not updated in this PR. Grafana applies environment-variable overrides by iterating the keys that exist in the loaded ini files, so a key that is absent from defaults.ini cannot be set via `GF_AUTH_ANONYMOUS_DEVICE_LIMIT` — operators running in containers (the common case) would silently get the default of 0/unlimited. The option is also undocumented, so users have no way to discover it or its semantics (0 = unlimited).

findings.title: Raw ErrDeviceLimitReached returned from Authenticate yields an opaque 500 to the user
findings.body: `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is a plain `fmt.Errorf` value, and it is returned directly from `Anonymous.Authenticate`. The authn broker/HTTP layer has no mapping for it, so an anonymous visitor who is rejected because of the device limit receives a generic internal-server-error rather than a meaningful status/message. Use an `errutil` error with an appropriate status (e.g. 429/403) and a user-facing message so the rejection is diagnosable and does not look like a server fault.

findings.title: Provider signature changes are not reflected in the DI/wire configuration
findings.body: `ProvideAnonymousDeviceService` now takes `sqlStore db.DB` instead of `anonStore anonstore.AnonStore`, and `anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore` gained a second `deviceLimit int64` parameter. The wire configuration (pkg/server/wire.go and generated wire_gen.go), which registers `anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore` and binds it to `anonstore.AnonStore`, is not part of this PR. Unless those files are updated, wire generation/compilation fails (no provider for `int64`, and the old call `ProvideAnonDBStore(sqlStore)` no longer matches). Also, because the store is now constructed inside the service, the previously injectable `anonstore.AnonStore` binding becomes dead/unsatisfiable for any other consumer.

findings.title: Device tagging moved onto the synchronous authentication path
findings.body: `TagDevice` was previously executed in a background goroutine with its own 2-minute timeout; it is now called inline during `Authenticate`. Every anonymous request whose device ID is not in the 29-minute local cache now performs a `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM anon_device` (when a limit is configured) plus an upsert before the response can proceed, adding database round-trips to request latency. With randomly generated device IDs (cache misses on every request) this turns each anonymous request into at least two synchronous DB statements, which is a cheap amplification vector against the database. Consider keeping the write asynchronous and only performing the limit check synchronously, or caching the count.

findings.title: Device-limit tests do not cover the important paths
findings.body: `TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit` only asserts that a second, new device is rejected. There is no test that an *existing* device can still be refreshed once the limit is reached (the main purpose of `updateDevice`), no test that a device whose `updated_at` is older than the 30-day window behaves as intended, and no test of the service-level behaviour (the local-cache interaction in `tagDeviceUI`, which currently lets rejected devices through on subsequent requests). These are the cases most likely to regress.

findings.title: anonymousDeviceLimit is typed as `undefined` on the boot config and can never actually be undefined
findings.body: `anonymousDeviceLimit = undefined` has no type annotation, so TypeScript infers the property type as `undefined` on `GrafanaBootConfig`; any consumer writing `config.anonymousDeviceLimit > 0` will fail to type-check even though the value is a number at runtime. Additionally the backend DTO field is a non-pointer `int64` with no `omitempty`, so the frontend always receives a number (0 when no limit is configured) and the declared `number | undefined` in `GrafanaConfig` is misleading. Annotate the field (`anonymousDeviceLimit: number | undefined = undefined;`) or make the type `number` to match what the server actually sends.
